overview.title: Reading David-Horodok Through Its Memorial Book
overview.summary: David-Horodok was a Jewish community with religious institutions, schools, political movements, banks, trades, and organized communal life. The memorial book traces this world through changing rule and wartime upheaval, the German occupation, murder and deportation, and the efforts of individuals to hide, escape, fight, and survive. It also follows the community after destruction: survivors returned, rebuilt lives, pursued perpetrators, and preserved names and testimony. Exploring these paths will help readers see both the richness of prewar life and the human choices and losses recorded in its aftermath.

paths.title: What kind of Jewish community was David-Horodok?
paths.description: This path introduces the institutions and everyday structures that made David-Horodok a functioning Jewish community. By the end, readers will see a town shaped by religious practice, education, economic cooperation, and mutual aid.
paths.question: How did communal life work before the destruction?

steps.title: A self-organized community
steps.summary: The memorial book describes David-Horodok as an organized Jewish settlement and says that its community became independent under tsarist rule. It also records a town administration elected every three years before Russian rule, showing that communal organization included civic as well as religious structures. paths.title: How did politics and changing borders shape the town?
paths.description: This path follows socialist, Zionist, and communal political activity alongside the successive authorities that governed David-Horodok. It helps readers understand why political ideas, migration plans, and state power mattered so deeply to local lives.
paths.question: How did residents respond to political change before the Holocaust?

steps.title: Political movements take root
steps.summary: During the revolutionary period of 1905, a small Bund group was organized in David-Horodok, and Poale Zion also existed there. The memorial book thus presents political life as plural, with competing socialist and Zionist visions active in the town. [event_candidate_61032a7ea799c1d014ada76e, mention_749d32a48606275263727c6a]

steps.summary: The town had a Zionist youth organization, a local Zionist committee, and a General Zionist organization active in Keren Hayesod. paths.title: How did occupation become persecution and mass murder?
paths.description: This path moves from military occupation and forced labor to roundups, ghettos, and killings. It shows how the memorial book records destruction through both collective events and individual victims.
paths.question: How was David-Horodok’s Jewish population persecuted and destroyed?

steps.title: Occupation and coercion
steps.summary: After German forces occupied the town, Jewish men were taken to work outside it, while women and children were ordered to leave within one hour. The book also records Jewish men being assembled at the market opposite the Catholic church for labor, illustrating how occupation entered ordinary public spaces. [event_candidate_69f31fb2912186171604778c, event_candidate_76016559c7a50207c9e5d29c, mention_ea655fdcc242a18799afa6d8]

paths.title: How did people resist, hide, and survive?
paths.description: This path follows the different possibilities recorded in the book: escape from ghettos, help from non-Jewish people, partisan warfare, and dangerous attempts to cross borders. It emphasizes survival as a series of individual acts under extreme constraint, not a single experience.
paths.question: What forms did survival and resistance take?

paths.title: What happened to families after the destruction?
paths.description: This path brings the story from wartime loss into liberation, return, rebuilding, and justice. It helps readers understand that survival involved fractured families, physical return to a devastated town, and the creation of new lives elsewhere.
paths.question: How did survivors carry family and community forward?

steps.title: Families under persecution
steps.summary: The book recalls families separated by arrest, deportation, and murder, including Golda Finkelstein and her mother Yentl in the Sarny Ghetto. Another narrator remembers being with parents during the final night in the ghetto, while recalling a wider family of a wife, four children, parents, siblings, and sisters. [mention_57ea468ae2cbc4593d4a34b6, mention_e31ead8de912229c1ea48219, mention_5b7f2036ccbced2a8866343c, mention_7c77167e6b1e72b26ab46d46]

paths.title: How does the memorial book remember David-Horodok?
paths.description: This path explores how testimony preserves names, family links, religious memory, survival accounts, and the pursuit of perpetrators. Readers will learn to approach the memorial book as a source of remembrance whose accounts must be read with attention to who is speaking and what is being preserved.
paths.question: What does the memorial book choose to remember?

steps.title: Names within a destroyed community
steps.summary: The book names victims such as Aharon Hershel Dorzin, Reuven Kaluzhny, Abraham Slutsky, and members of the Gloiberman family. These names restore individuality to people otherwise represented only within accounts of mass murder. [mention_37ec6542f311cddfe0183c2e, event_candidate_3fa4a8ac22d01f333860623e, event_candidate_e3a08578571acfa188df738c, mention_49787841f5f45bf73f530b87]

steps.title: Memory through religious and family traditions
steps.summary: A narrator’s grandmother is remembered recounting a custom of preparing a memorial candle, while other passages preserve synagogue practice, rabbis, and family relationships. The book therefore remembers David-Horodok not only through its destruction, but also through inherited rituals and stories. steps.title: Survivor testimony as historical evidence
steps.summary: The memorial book preserves first-person accounts of hiding, escape, partisan service, parents preparing for death, and return after liberation. Such testimony conveys lived experience and memory; it should be read as the account of the named witness or narrator, rather than as an assumption that every detail represents the whole community. [mention_850823aeb0422b71fde81ae9, mention_864075f2928fde6b382d68d2, event_candidate_352f0edd7088a295af7f82cc, event_candidate_e3950c91e4fa5606b26a3c6c]
